topic_summary: Analysis of the Renaissance reconstruction of Classical Latin, examining the epistemological contest between medieval Latin as a living drifted vernacular and humanist Classical Latin as a textual ideal recovered from ancient sources. The core question is whether the reconstructed form was reachable through continuous linguistic evolution or required a discontinuous leap to a separate symbolic kernel.

key_entities: Medieval Latin users (living vernacular practitioners, no textual purism)
Humanist reconstructors (philological scholars seeking Classical purity)
Lorenzo Valla (descriptive philologist, Classical Latin advocate)
Reformist critics (Poliziano, Erasmus - adaptive vitality advocates)
Classical Latin corpus (Cicero, Virgil - textual authority)
key_tensions: Living language vs textual artifact (medieval practice vs humanist reconstruction)
Continuity vs rupture (evolutionary drift vs discontinuous recovery)
Prescriptive vs descriptive (Ciceronian rules vs Valla's usage-based approach)
Natural vs artificial (Dante's vernacular vs grammatica distinction)
Rigid reconstruction vs adaptive use (Bembo's oath vs Erasmus's pragmatism)
key_mechanisms: Philological reconstruction (ad fontes methodology, orthographic purging)
Dual register maintenance (purified publication vs vernacular-influenced practice)
key_absences: Phonological evidence (how Classical Latin actually sounded - no living speakers)
Non-elite medieval Latin users (ecclesiastical and administrative practitioners outside humanist circles)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The shared commitment to 'correct Latin' as the legitimate form of the language, with contested readings of what that correctness consists of and how it is accessed
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Medieval users ground authority in living practice and ecclesiastical tradition; humanists ground authority in textual fidelity to Classical sources
commitment_system_recognition.candidate_pattern: Interpretive Tradition (contested readings of a shared linguistic kernel)

readings.commitment: Correct Latin is the living evolved form shaped by continuous use, vernacular influence, and practical needs
readings.authority_grounding: Living practice, ecclesiastical tradition, natural linguistic evolution
readings.expected_structural_delta: Low extractiveness (no enforcement cost for natural drift); beneficiary is the practicing community; victim is textual purity; continuity with medieval practice

readings.commitment: Correct Latin is the Classical form recoverable through philological analysis of ancient texts
readings.authority_grounding: Textual evidence from Cicero and Virgil, philological methodology (ad fontes)
readings.expected_structural_delta: Moderate extractiveness (requires scholarly apparatus and orthographic discipline); beneficiary is humanist elite; victim is vernacular-influenced users; rupture from medieval practice but claims historical continuity with Classical period

readings.commitment: Correct Latin is the prescriptive ideal defined by strict Ciceronian imitation, excluding all post-Classical developments
readings.authority_grounding: Cicero's corpus as exclusive authority, oath-bound fidelity to textual precedent
readings.expected_structural_delta: High extractiveness (requires constant policing of vocabulary and forms, dual register maintenance); beneficiary is Ciceronian elite (Bembo, Sadoleto); victim is linguistic vitality and adaptive capacity; complete rupture from both medieval practice and natural language evolution

axiom_contradictions.basis: Living drift treats language as naturally evolving through use (Dante's 'natural' vernacular principle); prescriptive ideal treats language as artificial construct bound by textual rules. No single framework can hold both that linguistic correctness emerges from living practice AND that it requires rigid conformity to historical textual precedent.

Textual recovery assumes Classical Latin is a recoverable historical form accessible through philological reconstruction; living drift assumes correctness is defined by current practice. No single framework can hold both that the correct form is what ancient texts preserve AND that the correct form is what living users produce.

axes.human_readable: Living Drift Reading (Medieval Latin as Natural Evolution)
axes.structural_delta: Latin as living language shaped by continuous vernacular influence and practical ecclesiastical/administrative use
axes.primary_observable: Orthographic variation in medieval manuscripts (e for ae, palatalization effects); vocabulary borrowing from Vulgate and Germanic sources; vernacular pronunciation patterns in handwritten documents
axes.selection_reason: First reading of contested kernel; establishes baseline of medieval practice before humanist intervention

axes.structural_delta: Classical Latin as recoverable historical form accessed through ad fontes philological methodology
axes.primary_observable: Humanist orthographic reforms (ae written in full, t/c distinction); Valla's descriptive philology; dual register maintenance (purified publication vs vernacular-influenced practice)
axes.selection_reason: Second reading of contested kernel; moderate extractiveness; claims continuity with Classical period while rupturing from medieval practice

axes.structural_delta: Correct Latin as prescriptive ideal requiring strict Ciceronian imitation and exclusion of all post-Classical developments
axes.primary_observable: Bembo's oath to use no non-Ciceronian words; refusal to use specific verb forms absent from Cicero's corpus; Erasmus's critique of rigidity in Ciceronianus
axes.selection_reason: Third reading of contested kernel; highest extractiveness; reveals the limit case of textual authority over living practice

axes.structural_delta: Absence of phonological evidence for how Classical Latin actually sounded, creating irreducible uncertainty in reconstruction
axes.primary_observable: Gap between textual evidence and acoustic reality; reliance on orthographic inference and Romance language comparison
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: structural absence feeding into both reconstruction readings but lower centrality than the readings themselves

axes.human_readable: Dual Register Mechanism (Purified Publication vs Vernacular Practice)
axes.structural_delta: Humanists maintained two distinct Latin registers: purified Classical for publication, vernacular-influenced for practical handwritten use
axes.primary_observable: Orthographic differences between published humanist works and their handwritten correspondence; vernacular pronunciation in practical documents
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: downstream mechanism of textual_recovery_reading with limited independent structural yield

deferred_axes.structural_delta: Absence of phonological evidence for Classical Latin pronunciation
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Structural absence feeding into reconstruction readings but lower centrality; captured indirectly through the readings' reliance on textual rather than acoustic evidence

deferred_axes.structural_delta: Humanist maintenance of purified publication vs vernacular-influenced practice registers
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Downstream mechanism of textual_recovery_reading with limited independent yield; the dual register is evidence of the reading's extractiveness rather than a separate constraint

omegas.description: Is the textual_recovery_reading genuinely continuous with Classical Latin (as humanists claimed) or is it a discontinuous reoccupation of a symbolic kernel? The absence of living speakers makes this epistemologically undecidable—we cannot verify whether reconstructed pronunciation, syntax, and usage match Classical practice or constitute a new artificial language.
omegas.source: Core kernel contest; phonological_absence deferred axis

omegas.description: Does Erasmus's adaptive position (Ciceronianus critique) represent a fourth reading that synthesizes textual authority with linguistic vitality, or does it collapse into textual_recovery_reading with pragmatic modifications? His position may warrant separate analysis if the binary between reconstruction and prescription is insufficient.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory) - reformist critics as potential separate reading

omegas.description: The humanist project displaced vernacular languages from elite discourse. Is this displacement a separate snare (extracting from vernacular literary development) or a consequence of the readings already identified? The victim set may extend beyond Latin users to vernacular language communities.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan) - Dante's vernacular advocacy vs humanist Latin valorization

omegas.description: Medieval Latin users outside humanist circles (parish priests, notaries, merchants) are absent from the analysis. Their practice may constitute a separate reading or may simply be living_drift_reading at different social registers. Insufficient evidence to classify.
omegas.source: Extraction absence: non-elite medieval Latin users

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. The kernel/reading decomposition successfully captures the epistemological contest. The three readings represent genuinely distinct commitments about what 'correct Latin' consists of and how it is accessed. Axiom contradictions confirmed: no single framework can hold both that correctness emerges from living practice AND that it requires textual fidelity, nor that the correct form is recoverable from texts AND defined by current use.
